title: Re-covering a headboard in linen
subtitle: Strip an existing headboard, cut new linen fabric with a generous wrap allowance, and staple it under even tension with mitre-folded corners
excerpt: How to re-cover a fabric-upholstered headboard in linen or other woven fabric. Covers removing old fabric, inspecting and repairing the base padding, cutting the new fabric, applying even tension while stapling, and forming neat corners.
sourceNotes: Traditional upholstery and soft furnishing practice, public domain. UK trade upholstery practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The structural layer of a padded headboard, typically an MDF or plywood board with a foam and wadding or wadding pad glued to the front face. When re-covering, the base and padding are retained if sound; only the outer fabric is replaced.

The tautness applied to the fabric as it is pulled over the padding and stapled to the back of the board. Even tension produces a smooth, flat face with no sagging or bunching. The sequence is always to staple the centre of each side first, then work outward alternating between opposite sides, keeping the tension consistent throughout.

content.text: A headboard re-covered in linen gives a bedroom an immediate refresh without replacing the furniture. The work strips the old fabric, smooths the base padding, and staples new fabric over the
. INTERMEDIATE: getting tension consistent across the full width before stapling is the one skill to master.

Remove the headboard from the bed and lay it face-down on a protected surface. Use the staple remover to pull all the staples from the back and sides, working along the edge systematically. Remove the old fabric. Inspect the foam and upholstery wadding: if the foam is intact and firm, keep it; if it has compressed or crumbled at the edges, replace the damaged sections with new foam and re-glue.

Measure the full width and height of the headboard face. Add 100 mm wrap allowance on each of the four sides. Cut the linen to this total size. Check the grain is straight and perpendicular to the longest edge before cutting.

Lay the headboard face-down on the linen, centred with equal wrap on all sides. Fold the top edge of the linen over and staple the centre point of the top to the back of the board. Pull the bottom edge straight and firm and staple the centre of the bottom edge. Repeat at the centre of the left and right sides. From these these four points, work outward in short increments alternating between opposite sides to maintain even tension. Do not staple the corners yet.

At each corner, pull the fabric diagonally across the corner, folding one edge over and then the other in a neat mitre. Secure with staples. Trim any excess fabric bulk at the corner if the layers are too thick to fold flat. Finish the back by stapling a cambric or non-woven dust cloth over all raw edges and staple lines.

attrs.symptom: Fabric face is puckered or shows tension lines when installed
attrs.cause: The fabric was not pulled under consistent tension, or the grain was not aligned with the headboard edges when cutting.
attrs.fix: If the puckers are minor, they may relax over a few days. For significant puckers, remove the staples on the affected side, re-pull under firmer tension, and re-staple.

attrs.symptom: Linen frays at the staple line along the back edge
attrs.cause: Linen has a loose weave and frays readily where the fabric is folded over the board edge.
attrs.fix: Apply a thin bead of PVA fabric glue along the cut edge before folding. When dry, the glue stiffens the edge and prevents further fraying.
